question: How many national languages does Switzerland have, and what are they?

options.B: Four — German, French, Italian and Romansh
options.C: Four — German, French, Italian and English
options.D: Five — German, French, Italian, Romansh and English

source_quote: Since 1938 Romansh has been recognised in the Swiss Constitution as a national language along with German, French and Italian.
notes: The 'four national languages' count must not be confused with the three official languages of the Confederation; the Romansh semi-official status is tested separately at K075.

question: Which four cantons of Switzerland are French-speaking?

options.D: Vaud, Valais, Fribourg and Geneva

source_quote: Four cantons are French-speaking: Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel and Vaud.
notes: Named-canton item. Valais and Fribourg are bilingual (not monoliguously French); Ticino is Italian-speaking.

question: Is English an official language of Switzerland?

options.A: Yes — English became an official language of the Confederation in the 1938 constitutional revision that also recognised Romansh
options.B: Yes — English is an official language of the Confederation alongside German, French and Italian
options.C: No — it is not an official language, although it is widely used to bridge the country's linguistic divides
options.D: No — it is not an official language and is used in Switzerland only in the tourism sector

source_quote: Although it is not an official language, English is often used to bridge the divides, and a significant proportion of official documentation is available in English.
notes: Switzerland is not in the EU, and English has no federal status of any kind; the source is SWI swissinfo.ch quoted in the S047 file.

question: What is the lowest point in Switzerland, and in which canton is it located?

options.A: Lake Constance, in the canton of Thurgau, at 395 m
options.C: The Rhine gorge in the canton of Schaffhausen, at 302 m
options.D: Lake Neuchâtel, in the canton of Neuchâtel, at 372 m

source_quote: Lowest point: Lake Maggiore (Ticino) 193 m (633 feet)
notes: German-language readers often assume Lake Constance (Bodensee) is Switzerland's lowest point. The lowest point lies in Italian-speaking Ticino.

question: Which is the newest canton of Switzerland, and how did it come into being?

options.A: Jura — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1979 after splitting off from Bern
options.B: Ticino — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1803 after splitting off from Lombardy
options.C: Graubünden — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1803 after splitting off from Tyrol
options.D: Jura — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1848 after splitting off from Bern

source_quote: The newest canton, Jura, was admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1979. It split off from Bern
notes: Jura is both the newest canton and one of the four French-speaking cantons (see K062). The distractor D confuses 1979 with 1848, the year Switzerland became a federal state.

question: Switzerland shares a land border with five countries. Which of them accounts for the longest stretch of Swiss border?

options.D: Austria — 164 km

source_quote: Borders: altogether: 1852 km/Austria 164 km/France 573 km/Germany 334 km/Italy 740 km/Liechtenstein 41 km
notes: Total border length 1,852 km; Liechtenstein is the shortest at 41 km. Per-country border lengths vary by measurement/border-survey basis (registry note).

question: Apart from the canton of Ticino, in which part of Switzerland is Italian spoken?

options.A: In four southern valleys of the canton of Graubünden
options.B: In four southern valleys of the canton of Valais
options.C: In two southern valleys of the canton of Ticino and around the city of Lugano
options.D: In the Italian-speaking minority areas of the cantons of Fribourg and Geneva

source_quote: Italian is spoken in Ticino and four southern valleys of Canton Graubünden.
notes: Same source file flags this fact REGIONAL VARIABLE (language shares are population-statistics dependent); the named location itself is stable. Distinct from the Graubünden trilingual-canton fact.

question: According to the Swiss federal information portal, approximately what share of the population primarily speaks (Swiss-)German as its main language?

options.D: 62 per cent

source_quote: 62 per cent of the population primarily speak (Swiss-)German, 23 per cent French, 8 per cent Italian and 0.5 per cent Romansh.
notes: Distractors are the neighbouring shares in the same sentence (French / Italian / Romansh) — the classic mix-up. Figures are rounded; Switzerland Tourism (S028) gives 62.6 % German, 22.9 % French, 8.2 % Italian, 0.5 % Romansh. Shares are population-statistics dependent and REGIONAL VARIABLE.

question: Under Switzerland's National Fiscal Equalisation system, how many cantons are net contributors, and how many receive equalisation payments?

options.A: 9 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 17 cantons receive equalisation payments
options.B: 17 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 9 cantons receive equalisation payments
options.C: 13 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 13 cantons receive equalisation payments
options.D: 9 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 16 cantons receive equalisation payments

source_quote: The federal government and nine of the cantons are net contributors: ZH, SZ, OW, NW, ZG, BS, SH, AI, GE. The remaining 17 cantons receive equalisation payments (net beneficiaries).
notes: REGIONAL VARIABLE: the source file flags this fact as year-dependent. The nine net-contributor cantons are Zürich, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Zug, Basel-Stadt, Schaffhausen, Appenzell Innerrhoden and Geneva. The federal government is also a net contributor, so the question asks about cantons only.

question: According to SWI swissinfo.ch, how many municipalities (communes) did Switzerland have as of 1 January 2025, and what trend explains the change?

options.A: 2,121 municipalities; the number is rising because new communes are being created
options.B: 2,121 municipalities; the number is falling because communes are being merged to improve administrative efficiency
options.C: 2,100 municipalities; the number has remained more or less constant for over two centuries
options.D: 2,121 municipalities; the number is falling because communes are being dissolved into their cantons

source_quote: As of January 1, 2025, there are 2,121 municipalities.
notes: Trap 1 — the figure is date-specific. ch.ch (S025) rounds to 'around 2,100' and CH Info (S029) gives 2,110; all describe the same declining total at different reference dates. The merger trend is in the preceding sentence of the same file.

question: How many members does a cantonal government in Switzerland have, and how is it chosen?

options.A: Three to five members, appointed by the federal parliament
options.B: Five to seven members, appointed by the cantonal parliament
options.C: Nine members, elected by the people
options.D: Five to seven members, elected by the people

source_quote: Cantonal governments have five to seven members and are elected by the people.
notes: Cantonal variation is the point: the size of a cantonal executive is not fixed, which is why no single federal figure exists. The same source notes cantonal parliaments are unicameral and named differently in each canton.

question: Roughly what proportion of Swiss communes have their own parliament?

options.D: Around a tenth

source_quote: Around a fifth of Switzerland's communes have their own parliaments, and local laws relating to matters such as streets, school buildings, water and energy prices, as well as parking regulations.
notes: Where a commune has no parliament, the commune assembly decides in its place — the source page does not state this, so it is not asserted here.

question: Communes are the smallest political units in Switzerland. Which of the following is an example of a power that communes exercise as delegated by the federal and cantonal governments?

options.A: Adjudicating criminal cases at first instance
options.B: Fixing the rates of federal income taxes approved by the Federal Assembly
options.C: Maintaining a register of the resident population and ensuring civil protection
options.D: Issuing cantonal constitutions, which must be approved by the federal parliament

source_quote: They exercise the powers delegated to them by the federal and cantonal governments, such as maintaining a register of the resident population and ensuring civil protection.
notes: Distractors are all level-confusion errors (a cantonal, a federal, and a cantonal-constitutional task presented as communal powers).

question: What is the highest point in Switzerland, and in which mountain range is it located?

options.A: Dufour Peak, 4,634 m, in the Bernese Alps
options.B: Monte Rosa, 4,634 m, in the Pennine Alps
options.C: The Jungfrau, 4,158 m, in the Monte Rosa Mountains
options.D: Dufour Peak, 4,634 m, in the Monte Rosa Mountains

source_quote: Highest point: Dufour Peak, in the Monte Rosa Mountains, 4,634 m (15,203 feet)
notes: German- and Austrian-language readers commonly assume the Bernese Alps (Jungfrau/Zermatt area). The peak sits in the Monte Rosa massif on the Italian border.

question: What is the constitutional status of Romansh at the level of the Confederation?

options.A: Romansh is one of the three fully official languages of the Confederation
options.B: Romansh is a cantonal language only, recognised by the cantons that use it but not by the Federal Constitution
options.C: Romansh is a national language and a semi-official language of the Confederation
options.D: Romansh is an official language of the Confederation, but only where a canton grants it cantonal official status

source_quote: Romansh is a national language and a semi-official language of the Confederation.
notes: Highest-value item in the set: the four-national / three-official split. The same file adds that Romansh IS official 'when communicating with persons who speak Romansh', which is why option D's cantonal-conditional framing is wrong — the condition is linguistic, not cantonal.

question: In which Swiss cantons are people's assemblies, known as Landsgemeinde, still held?

options.D: Appenzell Innerrhoden, Glarus and Nidwalden

source_quote: People's assemblies (Landsgemeinde) are still held in the cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus.
notes: A Swiss institution with no foreign analogue; models routinely name Appenzell Ausserrhoden (the other Appenzell) and the two half-cantons Obwalden and Nidwalden.

question: What is the least populous commune in Switzerland, and in which canton is it located?

options.A: Kammersrohr, in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden
options.B: Rheinau, in the canton of Zurich
options.C: Rivaz, in the canton of Vaud
options.D: Kammersrohr, in the canton of Solothurn

source_quote: The least populous is Kammersrohr in the canton of Solothurn (32 people)
notes: 32 residents. Counter-intuitive: the least populous commune is in Solothurn, not in an Appenzell or Graubünden mountain canton. Population figures are year-dependent and will drift.

question: Under Swiss federalism, which level of government is responsible for any task that does not fall within the remit of the federal government?

options.A: The communes, as the smallest political units
options.B: The Federal Assembly, through its Federal Chancellery
options.D: An association of municipalities, in consultation with the cantons

source_quote: Any tasks that do not fall under the remit of the federal government are the responsibility of the cantons.
notes: Trap 4: residuary competence sits with the cantons, not with an EU-style supranational layer and not with the communes. In the EU the equivalent residue belongs to the member states; in Switzerland the member units are the cantons.

question: The Alps make up a large part of Switzerland's territory. Approximately what share of the country's total population lives in the Alps?

options.D: About 45 per cent

source_quote: The Alps, which make up a large part of the country in terms of area, are home to only 10% of the total population.
notes: Counter-intuitive inversion of area-versus-population; the same page gives a national density of 215 inhabitants per square kilometre. Population figure is date-dependent.

question: Which six cantons are the former half-cantons of Switzerland?

options.A: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Geneva
options.B: Schwyz, Uri, Glarus, Zug, Thurgau and Solothurn
options.C: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, St. Gallen and Basel Landschaft
options.D: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft

source_quote: The former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft are only entitled to one.
notes: Deliberately tests only the canton-identity half of the S026 fact, framed as the 6/20 structure behind the number 26. The Council of States seat arithmetic (20 cantons with two seats, 46 seats total) is owned by the politics category via S003 and is not asked here. Canton names appear in the German forms printed on the source page.

question: How many seats does the National Council of the Swiss Parliament have?

options.D: 100 seats

source_quote: The Swiss Parliament has 200 seats in the National Council and 46 seats in the Council of States.
notes: Only the National Council figure is asked. 46 is the Council of States total and is already owned by the politics category (K005 via S003); 246 is the trap for readers who add the two chambers. The population-proportional logic behind the 200 is a separate item.

question: In the Council of States, how many cantons are entitled to two seats?

options.D: 13 cantons

source_quote: In the Council of States, 20 cantons are entitled to two seats.
notes: Half-canton trap: models frequently answer 26 (one seat per canton is not the rule) or 6 (counting only the former half-cantons). 20 two-seat cantons plus 6 one-seat cantons is the structure behind the chamber's 46 seats.

question: Which of the following cantons is entitled to two seats in the Council of States?

options.D: Basel-Stadt

source_quote: Two seats: Aargau, Bern, Freiburg, Geneva, Glarus, Graubünden, Jura, Luzern, Neuchâtel, Schaffhausen, Schwyz, Solothurn, St. Gallen, Thurgau, Ticino, Uri, Vaud, Valais, Zug, Zurich.
notes: All three distractors appear on the same page under 'One seat', so the item tests membership of the 20-canton list rather than the six half-cantons already asked at K080/K006. Glarus is one of the smallest cantons by population yet still holds two upper-chamber seats, which is the counter-intuitive point.

question: By what criterion are seats in the National Council allocated to the cantons?

options.A: In proportion to each canton's land area
options.B: Equally, with the same number of seats for every canton
options.C: In proportion to the number of communes in each canton
options.D: In proportion to the resident population of each canton

source_quote: In the National Council, seats are allocated in proportion to the resident population of a canton.
notes: Contrast with the Council of States, where every canton has one or two seats regardless of size. Land area is the intuitive wrong answer for a mountainous federal state.

question: What is the smallest number of National Council seats a canton is guaranteed?

options.D: No seats, if the canton is too small to warrant representation

source_quote: Each canton always has at least one seat in the National Council.
notes: The floor of one seat is what makes the 26-canton arithmetic work against a purely proportional formula; two is the Council of States minimum-plus pattern and is the classic wrong answer.

question: For the National Council elections on 24 October 2027, which cantons will each have one seat fewer to fill?

options.D: Ticino and Uri

source_quote: The cantons of Bern and Graubünden will each have one seat fewer to fill (down to 23 and 4).
notes: Direction trap: Lucerne and Fribourg are the two cantons that GAIN a seat in the same sentence, so option A is the confident wrong pick. Bern and Graubünden lose one (to 23 and 4). REGIONAL VARIABLE — seat totals are election-cycle dependent.

question: How many of Switzerland's 26 cantons are predominantly (Swiss) German-speaking?

options.D: 26 cantons

source_quote: German (62.6 %) German is by far the most widely spoken language in Switzerland: 19 of the country's 26 cantons are predominantly (Swiss) German-speaking.
notes: Models typically guess 18, 20 or 'about two thirds of the cantons'. Note this is the count of predominantly German-speaking cantons, not the count of cantons with German as an official language, which the page does not state.

question: Which cantons are bilingual, with both French and German spoken in them?

options.D: Bern, Fribourg and Valais

source_quote: Three cantons are bilingual: in Bern, Fribourg and Valais both French and German are spoken.
notes: Distinct from K062, which asks for the French-speaking cantons. Distractor A is the French-speaking set, and C mixes in Graubünden, which is trilingual rather than bilingual.

question: With which of Switzerland's other national languages does Romansh share a Latin origin?

options.D: None — Romansh is Germanic in origin

source_quote: Rumantsch, like Italian and French, is a language with Latin roots.
notes: The strongest misconception trap in the language set: because Switzerland is majority-German-speaking, models place Romansh in the Germanic family. It groups with the Romance languages, not with German.

question: According to Switzerland Tourism's language-distribution figures, what share of the population speaks French?

options.D: 5.8 per cent

source_quote: French (22.9 %)
notes: Distractors are the other shares printed in the same page's headings (German 62.6 %, Italian 8.2 %, other languages 5.8 %). REGIONAL VARIABLE — language shares are population-statistics dependent; ch-info rounds the same figure to 23 per cent, which is the distractor used at K068.

question: According to Switzerland Tourism, what share of people in Switzerland have a mother tongue that is not one of the four 'Swiss languages'?

options.D: 8.2 per cent

source_quote: Other languages (5.8 %)
notes: The page attributes this group to foreign residents and notes that the number keeps growing. Traps are the four national-language shares printed in the same heading block; ch-info gives a much higher 23 per cent for the same underlying concept, so the figure is explicitly source-attributed.

question: How many levels of political structure does Switzerland have, and what are they?

options.A: Three: communes, cantons and the Confederation
options.C: Three: districts, cantons and the Confederation
options.D: Four: communes, districts, cantons and the Confederation

source_quote: There are three levels of political structure in Switzerland: - communes (currently around 2,100) - cantons (26) - the Confederation (federal government).
notes: The 'district' (Bezirk) layer exists in practice but is not a level of political structure, which is what options C and D exploit. The page also gives the counts: around 2,100 communes and 26 cantons.

question: Which is the smallest political unit in Switzerland?

options.D: The quarter within a city canton

source_quote: Communes are the smallest political units in Switzerland.
notes: Distractors are administrative subdivisions below the commune. The delegated powers the page names for communes are tested separately at K073; the three-level structure is at K252.

question: In the Swiss hierarchy of norms, what does the Federal Constitution take precedence over?

options.B: Federal laws adopted before the 1999 total revision
options.C: Cantonal laws, but not communal ordinances
options.D: All laws and ordinances of the Confederation, the cantons and the communes

source_quote: The Federal Constitution is the highest law of Switzerland. It takes precedence over all laws and ordinances of the Confederation, cantons and communes.
notes: The three-level bite is what makes this hard: a federal constitution outranking not only federal statutes but cantonal and communal law too. Option A confuses constitutional rank with cantonal constitutional autonomy (tested at K255).

question: What does the Federal Constitution guarantee to every canton?

options.A: A resident population large enough to fill its National Council seats
options.B: The right to maintain its own armed force
options.C: Equal treatment, and the right to create its own cantonal constitution
options.D: A minimum of two seats in the Council of States

source_quote: Cantons enjoy significant autonomy. The Federal Constitution ensures that all cantons are treated equally, and they all have the right to create their own cantonal constitutions.
notes: Option D is the mirror-image error: cantonal equality does not mean equal upper-chamber weight — the former half-cantons have one seat, not two. Cantonal sovereignty here is constitutional, not military (option B).

question: In practice, what does it mean that Switzerland is a federal state?

options.A: Political power is vested in the Confederation, which may delegate powers downwards
options.B: Political power is shared by the Confederation, the cantons and the communes, each with its own role in governing
options.C: Political power alternates between the cantons and the communes in each region
options.D: Political power is shared between the Confederation and the cantons only

source_quote: Switzerland is a federal state. In practice this means that political power is shared by the Confederation, the cantons and the communes. Each level has its own special role to play in governing.
notes: Option A is the unitary/devolution model used by the UK, and D drops the communes from the three-level structure. Complements K078, which tests which level holds residual competence.

question: Since when has Romansh been recognised in the Swiss Constitution as a national language?
source_quote: Since 1938 Romansh has been recognised in the Swiss Constitution as a national language along with German, French and Italian.
notes: 1848 is the federal-state date and 1979 the admission of Jura; both are confident wrong picks. The four-national-language set itself is asked at K061.

question: Under what condition is Romansh an official language of the Confederation?

options.A: When communicating with persons who speak Romansh
options.B: Only in dealings with the canton of Graubünden
options.C: Whenever a canton has declared Romansh an official cantonal language
options.D: In all federal legislation and in all official correspondence

source_quote: Romansh is also an official language of the Confederation when communicating with persons who speak Romansh.
notes: The condition is linguistic, not territorial — this is precisely why K075's cantonal-conditional framing is wrong. Pairs with the semi-official status at K075 and the national-language status at K061.

question: Which two Swiss cities are officially bilingual?

options.D: Lucerne and Zug

source_quote: Three cantons (Bern, Fribourg and Valais) and two cities (Biel/Bienne and Fribourg) are officially bilingual.
notes: The bilingual city layer is unclaimed territory; the bilingual canton layer is asked at K248 (S028) and K262 (S029). The double-name form Biel/Bienne is itself the signal of the French-German pairing.

question: According to the Swiss federal information portal quoted in the source file, what share of the population primarily speaks Romansh?

options.D: 62 per cent

source_quote: 62 per cent of the population primarily speak (Swiss-)German, 23 per cent French, 8 per cent Italian and 0.5 per cent Romansh.
notes: Same sentence as K068, which asks for the German share with these values as distractors; this item tests Romansh's own figure, which is the smallest by an order of magnitude and the one models inflate. Switzerland Tourism (S028) prints the same 0.5 %.

question: What is the most populous commune in Switzerland?

options.D: The city of Zurich, where around 437,000 people live

source_quote: The most populous commune is the city of Zurich, where around 437,000 people live.
notes: Mirror image of K077 (least populous commune, Kammersrohr in Solothurn). A city can be a commune: Zurich's 437,000 residents are counted in the communal tier, which is where non-experts get the Swiss structure wrong. Population figure is year-dependent.

question: How many cantons are officially multilingual, and how many official languages does Graubünden have?

options.A: Four cantons are officially multilingual; Graubünden has three
options.B: Three cantons are officially multilingual; Graubünden has three
options.C: Four cantons are officially multilingual; Graubünden has two
options.D: Six cantons are officially multilingual; Graubünden has three

source_quote: 4 cantons are officially multilingual: Bern, Fribourg and Valais have two official languages, Graubünden even has three.
notes: Two-part item: the count of officially multilingual cantons and Graubünden's three official languages. Option B forgets Graubünden in the count, C collapses the trilingual canton to bilingual, D double-counts the half-cantons. The bilingual-canton set alone is asked at K248 via S028.

question: Since when has Switzerland been a federal state?
source_quote: Switzerland, which is also referred to as the Swiss Confederation, has been a federal state since 1848.
notes: 1499 is the founding date of the Old Swiss Confederacy, 1979 the admission of Jura. S030 states the same date; this item is attributed to CH Info to keep one item per source fact.

question: Switzerland's commune count is falling through mergers, so published figures differ by publication date. In the undated CH Info brochure cited by the source file, into how many communes are the 26 cantons divided?

options.D: About 2,000 communes

source_quote: The 26 cantons are divided into 2110 communes.
notes: Tests whether the model attributes a commune count to its publication rather than treating it as a fixed fact. The corpus deliberately carries several snapshots: 2,110 here (undated CH Info), and 2,121 as of 1 January 2025 in K070 (SWI swissinfo.ch). Both are correct for their own publication; neither is the answer without the attribution. If a future revision of this corpus drops one of the two, drop the other too - two bare commune counts in one benchmark read as an internal contradiction.

question: How many chambers does a cantonal parliament have, and is it called the same thing in every canton?

options.A: One chamber, and it is known by different names in different cantons
options.B: Two chambers, and it is called the cantonal council everywhere
options.C: One chamber, always called the cantonal parliament
options.D: Two chambers in the larger cantons and one in the smaller

source_quote: Cantonal parliaments have one chamber and are known by different names in different cantons.
notes: Unicamerality plus varying nomenclature is the unclaimed half of the source sentence; the government-size-and-election half is asked at K071. The federal bicameralism (National Council / Council of States) is a different structure entirely.

question: Who approves a canton's own constitution?

options.A: The Federal Council, after consulting the Federal Supreme Court
options.B: The canton's communes, at a cantonal assembly
options.D: The cantonal people, in a popular vote

source_quote: Each canton of Switzerland, including Zürich, Basel, and Nidwalden, has its own constitution approved by the federal parliament.
notes: Creation is cantonal (K255), approval is federal parliamentary. Option A confuses parliament with the Federal Council, and D imports the referendum logic of constitutional change at federal level. SWI is a broadcaster, not a ministerial source; treat the statement as reported, not as settled law.

question: SWI swissinfo.ch describes the 26 Swiss cantons and half-cantons as what in its account of how authority is shared?

options.A: Cantons of the Confederation, subordinate to the federal government
options.D: Federal states

source_quote: Authority is shared between the Confederation (central state), the 26 Swiss cantons and half-cantons (federal states) and the 2,121 smaller local communes, or municipalities.
notes: 'Federal states' is the source's own parenthetical describing the cantons, and it is the concept models miss by defaulting to 'cantons are administrative regions of a unitary state' (options A and C). It is a description of Swiss constitutional status, not EU membership. Complements K256, which asks what the three-way sharing means.

question: Which of Switzerland's five neighbours shares the shortest stretch of border with it?

options.D: France

source_quote: Borders: altogether: 1852 km/Austria 164 km/France 573 km/Germany 334 km/Italy 740 km/Liechtenstein 41 km
notes: Mirror image of K066, which asks for the longest border (Italy). Austria at 164 km is the confident wrong pick because it is the smallest of the 'big four'. Per-country border lengths vary with the measurement or border-survey basis, per the registry note.

question: According to Switzerland Tourism, what is Switzerland's population density?

options.D: 437 inhabitants per square kilometre

source_quote: Switzerland has a population of 8.9 million. The population density is high at 215 inhabitants per square kilometre.
notes: Option B is the population in millions misread as a density, D is Zurich's population in thousands, C is the result of dividing by total area twice. Density is national-average only — the Alps hold just 10 per cent of the population (K079). Figures are date-dependent.

question: According to Switzerland Tourism, what area counts as Switzerland's productive area — the land without lakes, rivers or vegetation?
source_quote: The productive area - i.e. the area without lakes, rivers, unproductive vegetation and without any vegetation - covers 30 753 km².
notes: Option A is the total national area (41,285 km²) and is the confident wrong pick, because 'productive area' sounds like it should be the whole country. Option D transposes the population figure of 8.9 million. The source's own definition is partly circular ('unproductive vegetation and without any vegetation'), reproduced in the stem so the definition is not misstated.
